items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
items.summary: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: Why Node.js HTTP backpressure must count bytes, not string length
items.summary: In Node.js, string.length counts UTF-16 code units, not bytes. When Node's HTTP OutgoingMessage buffered a write, it added data.length to the counters that drive backpressure, so multi-byte response bodies were under-counted by 2× for two-byte characters and 3× for most CJK text. write() kept returning true after the buffer was past its high-water mark, and the server paused the socket later than it should. My fix, nodejs/node#66039 (in review), counts bytes instead. When you write to a response faster than the network can send, data queues in memory. Backpressure is how Node tells you to slow down: response.write() returns false once the buffer reaches its highWaterMark, and you're expected to wait for 'drain'. Internally, Node also tracks a per-connection total to pause the TCP socket and the HTTP parser when too much output is queued. Both decisions depend on one number: how much data is buffered. If that number is wrong, backpressure is wrong. items.title: Localhost is not authentication: fixing a CWE-306 webhook in an AI agent framework
items.summary: Binding a server to 127.0.0.1 keeps the internet out. It does not keep out the other programs on the same machine. In NanoClaw, an AI agent framework, a loopback webhook that relays chat-gateway events accepted any local POST, so any unprivileged process could forge button clicks into the agent's response pipeline. That's CWE-306, missing authentication for a critical function, rated CVSS 6.6. I wrote a fix (#3065). The maintainers then shipped a simpler fix (#4013) that credited it, and comparing the two is the most useful part of this story. The issue (#2970) was reported by security researcher YLChen-007. NanoClaw's chat bridge started a small HTTP server on 127.0.0.1: /webhook to receive events forwarded from the chat gateway (Discord, in this case). Every POST body went straight into the event handler, and the loopback address was the only trust boundary. So any local process could send a forged GATEWAY_INTERACTION_CREATE payload, and the agent would treat it as a real user clicking a button: approving an action, answering a question, choosing an option. items.title: A Wi-Fi QR code is just a text string. Here is the format (and the escaping that trips people up)
items.summary: When a guest scans a Wi-Fi QR code and their phone says "Join CafeGuest?", there is no app, no link and no server involved. The QR code holds one short line of plain text, and the phone's camera knows how to read it. Once you know that line, you can generate Wi-Fi codes from any language with any QR library. WIFI:T:WPA;S:CafeGuest;P:welcome2026;; Field Meaning Values T: Security type WPA (covers WPA/WPA2/most WPA3), WEP, or nopass S: Network name (SSID) Case-sensitive P: Password Leave out for nopass H: Hidden network true only if the SSID is not broadcast Each field ends with ; and the whole string ends with an extra ;, which is why it finishes with ;;. What happens if your password is pass;word? The phone reads P:pass, sees the ;, and thinks the password field is over. The guest gets a vague "could not join" error. The special characters \, ;, ,, : and " must be escaped with a backslash, in both the SSID and the password: function escapeWifi(value) { return value.replace(/([\\;,:"])/g, '\\$1'); } function wifiPayload({ ssid, password = '', type = 'WPA', hidden = false }) { let s = `WIFI:T:${type};S:${escapeWifi(ssid)};`; if (type !== 'nopass') s += `P:${escapeWifi(password)};`; i

items.summary: You take a full-page screenshot, open the PNG, and the top of the page looks fine. Further down there are grey rectangles, empty cards and blank gaps where product photos should be. This is one of the most common headless-browser questions, and the usual answers ("add a delay", "wait for network idle") do not fix it. items.title: BullMQ for Beginners: Background Jobs That Actually Scale
items.summary: Some work should not happen inside a web request. Sending a welcome email, generating a PDF, resizing an image, or processing a payment webhook — if any of these run slowly, your user waits. BullMQ solves this by moving the work into a queue backed by Redis, so your API can respond instantly and the heavy work happens in the background. The pattern is simple: a producer adds jobs, workers process them. import { Queue, Worker } from 'bullmq'; const emailQueue = new Queue('emails', { connection: { host: 'localhost', port: 6379 }, }); // Producer: add a job from your API route await emailQueue.add('welcome', { userId: 42, email: 'a@example.com' }); // Worker: process jobs somewhere else const worker = new Worker('emails', async (job) => { await sendWelcomeEmail(job.data.email); }, { connection: { host: 'localhost', port: 6379 } }); BullMQ adds the features that make queues production-ready: automatic retries with backoff when a job fails, delayed jobs that run later, rate limiting, job priorities, and a dashboard to see what is stuck. Your app feels instant even on a slow network. Here is the whole idea in a few lines: import useSWR from 'swr'; const fetcher = (url) => fetch(url).then((res) => res.json()); function UserProfile({ id }) { const { data, error, isLoading } = useSWR(`/api/users/${id}`, fetcher); if (isLoading) return Loading... ; if (error) return Something went wrong. ; return {data.name} ; } That is it. items.title: Background jobs in Node.js in five minutes, without Redis
items.summary: TL;DR: SureQ is a job queue for Node.js and TypeScript with retries, schedules, dead letters and real delivery guarantees. One npm install, zero runtime dependencies, no extra server. Run the example below and you'll have a working queue before your coffee cools. Every Node.js app ends up needing background work: send the welcome email, resize the upload, sync the customer, run the nightly report. The usual answer is a queue library plus a Redis server, and suddenly your "quick feature" comes with infrastructure to provision, secure and monitor before a single job can run. SureQ takes a different route. items.title: Idempotency keys for POST APIs in Node.js: retry a payment without charging twice
items.summary: A client sends POST /charges, the network drops the response, and the client retries. Without protection, the server runs the charge twice. An idempotency key fixes it: the client generates a unique key per operation (usually a UUID) and sends it in an Idempotency-Key header on every attempt. The server stores the result of the first attempt under that key and replays it for retries. Three more rules make it safe. Reject the same key with a different request body (a client bug, not a retry). Return 409 if a retry arrives while the first attempt is still running. Release the key when the server fails with a 5xx error or an exception, so the retry can run for real. Tested Node.js with node:sqlite below. AI will change how applications are designed and how developers work, but the foundations of enterprise software engineering will remain critical. items.title: Server-driven rendering eliminates client bundle bloat and streamlines web application data fetching
items.summary: React Server Components (RSC) represent a paradigm shift in React application architecture by allowing components to render exclusively on the server and stream serialized UI payloads to the client. This approach eliminates large dependency libraries from client JavaScript bundles, enables direct database access without separate REST or GraphQL API layers, and eliminates client-side data fetching waterfalls. However, Server Components cannot use browser APIs, React state hooks like useState, or event listeners like onClick, requiring developers to explicitly declare interactive UI elements as Client Components using the 'use client' directive. For years, single-page application (SPA) architectures forced developers to choose between heavy client-side JavaScript bundles and complex data fetching patterns. Traditional Client-Side Rendering (CSR) requires browsers to download massive JavaScript bundles before executing data requests, leading to slow Initial Page Loads and visual layout shifts. items.title: Building a snippet keyboard for iPhone and a paste picker for the Mac menu bar
items.summary: I make Cutling, an app that keeps the text you type again and again (your address, bank details, an email signature, the reply you send every week) and pastes it with one tap. On iPhone and iPad it's a keyboard you switch to in any app; on the Mac it sits in the menu bar and Shift-Command-V opens a picker at your cursor. The code is open source under GPL-3.0 (GitHub). Here's how the two halves work, and the platform corners I ran into. A custom keyboard gets a textDocumentProxy, and inserting a snippet is one call: proxy.insertText(value). Images are different, because a keyboard can't insert an image into a text field. Cutling puts the image on UIPasteboard.general with its real type (it reads the type from the data with CGImageSourceGetType, so a GIF stays a GIF) and you paste it. That pasteboard write is why the keyboard asks for Full Access (RequestsOpenAccess in its Info.plist). Without it, a keyboard extension can't touch the pasteboard or the shared container at all. items.title: Running BiRefNet background removal in a Web Worker (and the CSP bug that almost bit us)
items.summary: Most online background removers make you upload your photo to a server, wait in a queue, and then either cap the export resolution or slap a watermark on it unless you pay for credits. When I built the background remover for Imagier, I wanted the whole pipeline to stay on the user's device. No uploads, no rate limits, and full PNG output right out of the box. Running a modern segmentation model like BiRefNet in the browser with ONNX Runtime Web is surprisingly doable now, but a few production details tripped us up along the way. Here is what actually worked. Inference and image decoding will freeze the main thread if you are not careful. items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI. Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital. items.title: Intuit Sells Mailchimp At About a Third of Its 2021 Purchase Price
items.summary: Intuit has agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion in cash and stock, less than one-third of the $12 billion it paid to acquire the email-marketing platform in 2021. The deal is set to close in early 2027. CNBC reports: In August Intuit started running Mailchimp as a distinct operating segment. The move was meant to give investors more transparency as the company tried to manage the unit for profitability, Sandeep Aujla, Intuit's finance chief, said at a September company briefing. Also on Thursday, Intuit announced stronger-than-expected earnings and revenue for its fiscal first quarter, which ended on Oct. 31. The company reported $2.91 in adjusted earnings per share on $4.35 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $2.70 per share and $4.31 billion in revenue. While Intuit's revenue increased 12% year over year, Mailchimp revenue declined 1% to $313 million. Analysts polled by StreetAccount had expected $314.4 million. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Azure Functions Integration Tests with Testcontainers and Azurite
items.summary: Which bugs in a queue-triggered Azure Function can a test with a mocked QueueClient never catch? Every bug that lives in the storage service or in the trigger binding instead of in your code: the encoding of the queue message, a blob container that doesn't exist yet, the naming rules for containers and blobs, and the JSON the worker has to deserialize. A test against a real Azurite container catches all four. With one container for the whole test run, the sample's six tests, two of them through a running Functions host, finish in under ten seconds on my machine. The unit testing article from earlier this year is the baseline: business logic in a service class, the function class tested with fakes, and a first look at Testcontainers. This series picks up where it stopped. Part 1 stays with Azure Storage, queues in and blobs out; the later parts cover Cosmos DB, Service Bus, architecture rules, contracts, load and CI. The code is in the companion repo, on .NET 10 with the isolated worker, xUnit v3 and Testcontainers 4.16. The repo moved to those versions after the unit testing article, so that article's code no longer matches it line for line. An API puts orders on the orders queue.

Only about half of parents think their teen uses them at all. We're building TeenCue, parental controls for AI. The idea is simple: let a parent know when one of their kid's AI chats may need a closer look, by topic and concern level, without ever showing the parent what was typed. On a computer that's a browser extension problem. On an iPhone it's much harder, and this post is about how we approached it. On iOS, third-party apps are sandboxed. There is no supported way for one app to read what happens inside another app, and that's a good thing. It also means a parental controls app can't see what a teen types into the ChatGPT, Gemini or Character AI apps. items.summary: Disclosure: I work on ClearWhirl, an iPhone app that works out what is in your photo library on the device, with no upload. Places is one of its features. Every photo with a location carries a latitude and longitude. Turning that into "Lisbon, Portugal" normally means CLGeocoder, which sends the coordinates to Apple's servers and is rate limited. For an app whose promise is that your library never leaves the phone, and which has to do it for thousands of photos, that was a non-starter. We replaced it with one bundled binary file, memory-mapped, and plain geometry. This is how it works. PHAsset.location is metadata. No new permission is needed beyond the photo library access you already have, and no pixel is read. That is the first privacy win: you are using data the library already holds. What you do with the coordinates then decides whether it stays private. Regions: Natural Earth 1:10m admin-1 borders (public domain), simplified to about 330 m so the file stays small. items.title: Google Signs Deal With Blue Origin to Send Satellite Data Centers Into Orbit
items.summary: Google has partnered with Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin to launch satellite-based AI data centers into orbit as part of its experimental Project Suncatcher initiative. "Engadget reports: Each of these satellites will be equipped with "roughly the capacity of a data center rack" and will enter into a sun-synchronous orbit via heavy-lift New Glenn rockets. The rocket will carry several Google tensor processing units, the company's proprietary AI chips, along with data center servers. The first launch isn't scheduled until early 2029, so we have a couple of years to see if this whole project even works. This is an experiment that Google calls a "long-term moonshot" to see if it's possible to put AI infrastructure in space by "tapping into the abundant solar power in orbit." The benefits of this would be massive. Data centers here on Earth are notorious hogs, with their snouts all over electricity grids, land and cooling systems. The hope is that the harsh vacuum of the cosmos will be a better fit for the technology. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Xcode Instruments in Practice: Profiling and Optimizing iOS Apps
items.summary: Most performance bugs I've chased in production iOS apps didn't come from code that was obviously slow. They came from code that was fine with test data and fell over with real data. Think of a list that scrolls smoothly with 20 items and stutters with 2,000, or a screen that opens instantly on a new iPhone and takes a second on a three-year-old one. A sort that runs on the main thread "because it's fast", until someone's account has eight years of history. You can't find these by reading code. You find them by measuring. Xcode Instruments is the tool Apple gives us for that. This article walks through the workflow I use: profile, investigate, optimize, verify. It uses real Swift 6 code and the Instruments features in current Xcode releases. The usual symptoms we're hunting: Slow screen transitions, where a push or sheet animates late or stutters. UI freezes, where the main thread is busy or blocked and taps don't register. High CPU use that drains battery and heats the device. Excessive memory allocations that cause churn, peak-memory spikes, and terminations. SwiftUI view bodies re-evaluating far more often than the data changes. items.title: The .NET Hot Path Field Guide: Measure, Shape, and Ship Faster Code
items.summary: Production performance work in .NET is rarely about discovering a secret API. It is about seeing the runtime as a moving system: requests enter, objects accumulate, work queues form, database calls wait, and small conveniences become repeated costs. The useful question is not “How do I make this code faster?” It is “Which work happens often enough, under enough load, to matter?” This field guide focuses on the advanced, repeatable practices that tend to improve real .NET services: measuring first, designing hot paths deliberately, controlling allocation, respecting asynchronous boundaries, and making data access predictable. A hot path is code whose cost is amplified by frequency, concurrency, or both. A method that takes 200 microseconds may be irrelevant when called once per hour and disastrous when called thousands of times per second. Start with observable symptoms: Rising p95 or p99 endpoint latency Allocation rates that trigger frequent garbage collections Thread pool queue growth Database connection pool exhaustion CPU use that rises nonlinearly with traffic Lock contention or long request wait times Use the right tool for the suspected failure mode: | Question | Useful tool

items.title: Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 in .NET: Design Agents at the Boundary
items.summary: An AI agent is easy to demo when it has one tool, one prompt, and no consequences. Ask it to summarize a document, call a weather API, or draft a support reply, and the interaction feels almost magical. The engineering work begins when the agent can affect the world. Once it can create tickets, query customer records, issue refunds, modify infrastructure, or trigger a deployment, it is no longer simply a conversational feature. It becomes a component in a distributed system: probabilistic at its reasoning layer, deterministic at its boundaries, and accountable for every action it requests. Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 gives .NET teams a foundation for building this kind of application. Its value is not merely that it can connect a model to tools. Its more important promise is architectural: agents, tools, orchestration, memory, and execution can be represented as application components rather than improvised prompt logic scattered through controllers and services. The most useful way to approach the framework is boundary-first design. A language model can decide that a tool should be called. Moving from net10.0 to net11.0 changes the compiler, SDK, runtime, base class libraries, analyzers, container images, and often the assumptions embedded in a build pipeline. That breadth is precisely why .NET 11 should not be approached as a Friday-afternoon dependency bump. The useful question is not “What is new in .NET 11?” in isolation. MCP gives AI clients a standardized way to discover and call tools, read resources, and use reusable prompts. For C# teams, it offers an appealing path: wrap existing application services, databases, internal APIs, and operational workflows in a protocol designed for agent-driven interaction. items.title: Don't Abort the Whole Batch: Per-Photo Errors, Temp Files, and Cancel-Safe Exports in Swift
items.summary: A batch export that stops at the first bad photo is a frustrating kind of almost-done. Someone picked eighty pictures, the app processed forty, hit a file that wouldn't decode, and handed back nothing. Or worse: it left a half-written JPEG in Recents and no explanation of what happened. I build BatchMark, an iPhone app for finishing photos in batches. When a set is being watermarked or filtered, the export has to finish the photos it can, skip the ones it can't, and leave the phone no messier than it was before. This post is a teaching extract of that job structure, not the app's source. The image processing itself is out of scope. What matters here is how you run the job. The shape I keep coming back to has four parts: Treat each photo as its own unit of work, with its own result. Write to a temporary file first, and only move it when the write has finished. Keep going after a failure, and collect the errors. Honour cancellation between photos, and clean up anything you created. items.title: PHP Readies Critical Security Updates to Patch Another RCE Flaw
items.summary: PHP has released security updates addressing seven critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities across its supported versions, just four weeks after patches for the widely exploited PHP2Shell flaws. SecurityWeek reports: One of the security defects expected to be resolved is CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution (RCE) defect in the file-upload progress tracking functionality. The vulnerability was publicly disclosed two days after PHP2Shell made headlines. PHP's maintainers warned at the time that the security flaw can be triggered only under an unusual combination of configuration and code. "An application must set session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start(). Session upload progress must also still be enabled," PHP said last month. Noting that patches would be released as part of the regular update cycle, PHP developers recommended disabling session upload, a setting also listed as a mitigation for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two RCE bugs tracked as PHP2Shell. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: FCC greenlights rule allowing prisons to jam cellphone signals
items.summary: The Federal Communications Commission voted unanimously to allow state and local prisons to jam cellphones. In an announcement on Thursday, the FCC argues the rule will help combat an "influx of contraband cellphones" used to carry out crimes from prison. The company is looking to tap growing cybersecurity spending as the rapid adoption of AI creates new security risks and gives attackers new ways to exploit vulnerabilities. "AI tools are surfacing vulnerabilities faster than companies can patch them, and that is pushing customers to consolidate onto fewer platforms," said Catharine Trebnick, senior research analyst at Rosenblatt Securities. With the acquisition of Applied Compute, Palo Alto aims to offer a technology platform that helps customers securely train and deploy open-weight models as they expand their use of AI. items.summary: joshuark quotes a report from BleepingComputer: Microsoft is testing a new feature that lets enterprise IT administrators remotely lock stolen or lost Windows devices without wiping them. Named Remote Lock, this new feature is shipping to devices upgraded to Windows 11 Insider Preview builds in the Beta (Build 26320.10003) and Experimental (Build 26340.10013) channels. Admins can use Microsoft Intune custom configuration profiles to lock Microsoft Entra-joined, hybrid-joined, or MDM-enrolled devices that run Windows Enterprise, Education, or Pro. After the IT department remotely locks the device, the system can only be unlocked via Intune, since PINs, passwords, local admins, or web sign-ins will no longer work. Microsoft added that the user's credentials will remain valid and can still be used to sign into other devices that haven't been locked. "Windows signs out every active session, hides all sign-in options and shows a locked screen," said Windows Insider communications lead Stephen Lines. items.title: What three months of shipping an AlarmKit app taught me
items.summary: In late August we shipped a small iOS 26 app that turns calendar events into AlarmKit alarms: if an event title contains a keyword you registered, a real alarm rings some minutes before it, through Silent mode and Focus, until you stop it. I wrote up the launch-week lessons back then. This post is the other half: things that only showed up after real people had been using it for a few months. None of them are in the docs, and one of them came from a user report that ended with "I had to restart my phone". AlarmPresentation.Alert takes LocalizedStringResource values for the title and buttons. It is tempting to pass keys and let the system localize them. The full-screen alert is rendered by a system process, not by your app. When that process resolves a LocalizedStringResource, "the main bundle" is not your app. In our case the alarm came up showing the raw key — in our project the source language is Japanese, so English users saw Japanese. Other developers have reported the same thing after a device restart (FB20472264 on the Apple Developer Forums). items.title: Zero dependencies: notes on nRouter's Swift SDK
items.summary: Adding AI calls to an iOS or macOS app usually goes one of two ways. You hand-roll URLSession code and maintain it forever, or you pull in a client library that drags its own dependency tree along. The Swift guide for nRouter takes a narrower path: an official Swift package with zero third-party dependencies, built on URLSession and structured concurrency. Full guide: https://nrouter.ai/docs/sdks/swift It's a Swift Package Manager dependency, so setup is one line in Package.swift (or File → Add Package Dependencies in Xcode): dependencies: [ .package(url: "https://github.com/nRouterGateway/nrouter-sdk.git", from: "2.2.1") ] The client reads NROUTER_API_KEY from the environment, which suits CLI tools and macOS apps, or you pass the key directly on iOS: import NRouter let client = try NRouter(apiKey: "...") // or try NRouter() from env It talks to https://api.nrouter.ai/v1 and covers iOS 15+, macOS 12+, watchOS 8+ and visionOS 1+. A chat call takes a plain dictionary and awaits the result: let payload: [String: Any] = [ "model": "nrouter/auto", "messages": [["role": "user", "content": "Explain Swift concurrency."]], "max_completion_tokens": 512 ] let result = try await client.chatCom

items.title: How to Generate an APNs JWT Provider Token From a .p8 Key
items.summary: Originally published at https://bestlatestapps.com/blog/how-to-generate-an-apns-jwt-provider-token-from-a-p8-key/. Token-based push authentication is simpler than certificates once it works. Getting it to work the first time, though, usually involves a 403 InvalidProviderToken with no further explanation. APNs JWT generator builds and signs a correct token from your .p8 key, Key ID and Team ID, decodes it, counts down to expiry, and gives you a curl command to test against APNs. An APNs provider token is a JWT: Header: {"alg": "ES256", "kid": " "} Claims: {"iss": " ", "iat": } Each part is base64url-encoded without padding, joined with a dot, and signed using ECDSA on the P-256 curve with SHA-256. The base64url signature becomes the third part. The page does the signing with the browser's Web Crypto API and shows the decoded header and claims next to the result. Key ID: in Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles → Keys, and in the file name AuthKey_XXXXXXXXXX.p8 (the page reads it from the name when it can). items.title: macOS 27 quietly renamed the screenshot location key
items.summary: I'm Bazi, and I make Pizazoo, a screenshot organizer for Mac, iPhone and iPad. Pizazoo doesn't take screenshots. On the Mac it organizes the ones you take with Shift-Command-3, 4 or 5 (or apps like CleanShot X, Shottr and Xnapper) by watching the folders they save to. So "where does macOS save screenshots?" is a question my app has to answer correctly, and in Settings the System Screenshots row has a Change Location… button that changes the answer. On macOS 27 that button stopped working. You picked a folder, the app wrote the setting, restarted SystemUIServer like it always had, and the next screenshot saved exactly where it did before. On a Mac where nothing had set the new key, that meant the Desktop. No error, no failed write. The setting simply had no effect. The Terminal tip that most guides give, defaults write com.apple.screencapture location followed by killall SystemUIServer, has the same problem. On macOS 27 it runs cleanly and changes nothing. The folder was fine and the restart was fine. The key was the problem. macOS 27 reads the save location from a different key in the same com.apple.screencapture domain: location-screenshot. "Most Starlink satellites orbit at around 53 degrees to the equator, so the satellites bunch up over the mid-latitudes. These worldwide figures are approximate, based on a global grid over a single day," Accu Components spokesperson told Space.com in an email. "Skies near the equator are the quietest, with around 490 satellites." Not all of those satellites are visible to the naked eye, the researchers said in a statement. items.title: Switching LLMs mid-conversation is a ski-rental problem (30 minute read)
items.summary: Most work on routing between language models is centered on making sure the right model handles the right request. A classifier scores the request, then the request is routed to a cheap model if it is easy, and a frontier model if it is hard. For coding agents, this is only half of the problem. The second half of the problem is knowing when a running session should change model. This problem, which this post discusses, has a classic form: the ski-rental problem.

items.title: Unblockable communication with gravity (32 minute read)

items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
items.summary: A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone. That means that (a+b)+c is not always equal to a+(b+c). This post looks at what happens when integer addition, which is exact, is used.

items.title: Handing over humanity (22 minute read)
items.summary: Some AI experts believe that once we achieve superintelligence, humans will be permanently disempowered, and we shall all be ruled by an AI god. This might not be such a desirable outcome, as humans have a natural desire for freedom. The arrangement will probably not work, as keeping power responsive to human needs has required checks developed over centuries, sustained by repeated feedback from the real world and correction, and there's no reason to keep that equilibrium stable once humans have surrendered all control. Humans have the ability now to steer the technology in a way that will not lead to a complete replacement of human judgment.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.
